title: Tara's lament
hookLine: a widow runs toward the battlefield, and a son lights his father's pyre
carry: antyeshti, the last rite, and room to grieve

cards: Word reaches the palace: Vali is down. The monkeys who saw it want to run, or hide, or shut the gates against Rama. Tara doesn't.

She was the one who warned him, earlier that same day, and he didn't listen. Now she runs the other way, out of the city, past the frightened crowd, toward the place where her husband is lying with an arrow in his chest.
Her son Angada is with her.

teach.b: Tara reaches Vali and falls beside him, and Valmiki gives her lament in full. She speaks to Vali: you lie on the bare earth as if you loved it more than me. She speaks bitterly to Sugriva: now you have the kingdom.
She even begs Rama to let her follow her husband. In the middle of an adventure story, the poem stops for a widow's grief and lets it be angry.

Then Vali's last words. He speaks to Sugriva without anger now: fate caught us both, more or less. He asks him to raise Angada as his own son and to listen to Tara, who sees things before anyone else.
He puts Indra's golden necklace on his brother, and dies. Sugriva breaks. Now that he's won, he'd rather have his brother than the throne.
Rama, who fired the arrow, steadies them all and tells them to perform the rites.
And Angada lights his father's pyre.
This is antyeshti, the last rite, the final one of the samskaras that mark a Hindu life from birth to death. Most Hindus cremate.
Agni, the same fire that witnesses a wedding, receives the body and returns it to the elements, while the atman, the self, is understood not to die.
Traditionally a son lights the fire; today daughters and others often do too. Then come days set aside for mourning, often ten to thirteen, depending on the family.
Notice Valmiki's order: the grief first, full and untidy, then the rite. The tradition doesn't ask mourners to be neat.

how: Most Hindus cremate their dead; a son traditionally lights the pyre, though daughters and other relatives now often do, and a mourning period of around ten to thirteen days follows, by family custom. Tara is also honored as one of the panchakanya, five women named in a verse some recite in the morning.

p: Vali asks Sugriva to raise him
the last rite, at the pyre

s: Tara's grief is quiet and resigned
she's angry, asks Rama to kill her too, and speaks bitterly to Sugriva.
Vali, dying, asks Sugriva to care for Angada
and to listen to Tara's counsel.
he's crushed by it and says he'd rather have his brother alive.

games.q: a friend asks why Hindu families cremate. by today's story and teaching, what fits?
o: the atman doesn't die; fire returns the body to the elements, and family lights it with prayers.
it's only about saving space in cemeteries.
fire punishes the body for its mistakes.
games.why: Angada lit his father's pyre: antyeshti, the last of the samskaras, given after Tara's grief had its full say.

practice: Bring to mind a loss, large or small, yours or someone else's, without pushing it away. Breathe in and let the feeling be its real size; breathe out and let your body hold it.

If you pray, many Hindus remember the dead with a lamp and a quiet om shanti. And if grief ever turns into thoughts of hurting yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Tara. Vali's wise wife, mother of Angada, whose anger and grief fill today's lament after her husband falls.

orig.note: Sanskrit tārā: star. Vali's wife, mother of Angada, known for her wisdom.

carryVoice: Your line: antyeshti, the last rite, and room to grieve. Tara's grief came first, then Angada's fire. That's day five hundred eighty-seven.
